sections.title: 15 Interview Questions with Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What are microservices and when should you use them?

**Answer:** Microservices split an application into small, independently deployable services, each owning a business capability and database. Use when: team is large (>20 devs), need independent deployment cycles, different scaling needs per feature, need technology diversity. DON'T use for: small teams, simple applications, early-stage startups (start with monolith, extract later).

### Q2: How do microservices communicate?

**Answer:** (1) **Synchronous** — REST/gRPC. Simple but creates coupling. (2) **Asynchronous** — Message queues (Kafka/RabbitMQ). Decoupled, resilient. (3) **Event-driven** — Publish events, subscribers react. Best for loose coupling. Best practice: use async for most communication, sync only for queries needing immediate response.

### Q3: What is the Saga pattern?

**Answer:** Saga manages distributed transactions as a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions. Two types: **Orchestration** — central coordinator decides steps. **Choreography** — each service publishes events, others react. Example: Order→Payment→Inventory→Shipping. If Payment fails, compensate by cancelling Order. Advantages over 2PC: no distributed locks, better availability.

### Q4: How do you handle data consistency across microservices?

**Answer:** Accept **eventual consistency** — services will converge to consistent state. Techniques: (1) **Saga pattern** for distributed transactions, (2) **Event sourcing** — events as source of truth, (3) **CQRS** — separate read/write models, (4) **Outbox pattern** — write event + data in same local transaction, (5) **Change Data Capture (CDC)** — capture database changes as events.

### Q5: What is service discovery and why is it needed?

**Answer:** In dynamic environments (containers/cloud), service instances change frequently. Service discovery maintains a registry of available instances. **Client-side** (Eureka): client queries registry, chooses instance. **Server-side** (K8s): load balancer queries registry. Tools: Consul, etcd, Kubernetes DNS, AWS Service Discovery.

### Q6: Explain the Circuit Breaker pattern.

**Answer:** Prevents cascading failures when a downstream service is slow/down. States: **CLOSED** (normal), **OPEN** (fail fast, don't call), **HALF-OPEN** (test with one request). On 5 consecutive failures → OPEN. After 30s timeout → HALF-OPEN → success → CLOSED. Benefits: fast failure, protects calling service, gives downstream time to recover. Libraries: Netflix Hystrix, Resilience4j.

### Q7: How do you decompose a monolith into microservices?

**Answer:** (1) Identify bounded contexts (DDD), (2) **Strangler Fig pattern** — gradually replace parts, (3) Start with peripheral services (notifications, search), (4) Extract one service at a time, (5) Use **Anti-Corruption Layer** between old and new, (6) Keep shared database temporarily, split later, (7) Build CI/CD pipeline before splitting. Takes months/years.

### Q8: What is CQRS and when to use it?

**Answer:** Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate write model (normalized, business rules) from read model (denormalized, fast queries). Events link them. Use when: read/write patterns differ significantly, need multiple read projections, complex queries on normalized data are slow. Example: write to PostgreSQL, read from Elasticsearch (full-text search) + Redis (caching).

### Q9: How do you handle failures in microservices?

**Answer:** (1) **Circuit breaker** — stop calling failing service, (2) **Retry with backoff** — handle transient failures, (3) **Timeout** — don't wait forever, (4) **Bulkhead** — isolate resources per service, (5) **Fallback** — return cached/default data, (6) **Health checks** — detect unhealthy instances, (7) **Graceful degradation** — serve partial data if some services down.

### Q10: What is the API Gateway pattern?

**Answer:** Single entry point for all clients. Responsibilities: (1) Request routing, (2) Authentication/authorization, (3) Rate limiting, (4) Response aggregation, (5) Protocol translation, (6) Caching, (7) Logging/monitoring, (8) Load balancing. Variation: **BFF** (Backend-for-Frontend) — separate gateway per client type (mobile/web).Tools: Kong, AWS API Gateway, Envoy.

### Q11: How do you test microservices?

**Answer:** (1) **Unit tests** — test service logic, (2) **Integration tests** — test with real DB/dependencies, (3) **Contract tests** (Pact) — verify API contracts between services, (4) **Component tests** — test one service in isolation with mocked dependencies, (5) **E2E tests** — test complete flows (expensive, keep minimal), (6) **Chaos engineering** — inject failures to test resilience.

### Q12: What is the Outbox pattern?

**Answer:** Solves: how to atomically update database AND publish an event. Solution: write domain change + event in SAME local transaction to an outbox table. A separate process reads the outbox and publishes to message broker. Guarantees: if transaction commits, event will eventually be published. No dual-write problem.

### Q13: How would you handle distributed tracing?

**Answer:** Assign a unique **trace ID** at the entry point. Each service creates a **span** (unit of work). Propagate trace ID in headers (X-Trace-ID). Collect spans in a central system (Jaeger/Zipkin). Can visualize end-to-end request flow, identify bottlenecks, debug failures. Tools: OpenTelemetry (standard), Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray.

### Q14: What are the downsides of microservices?

**Answer:** (1) **Operational complexity** — deploy, monitor, debug N services, (2) **Distributed system challenges** — network failures, eventual consistency, (3) **Data management** — no joins across services, (4) **Testing complexity** — E2E tests are hard, (5) **Team coordination** — API contracts, backwards compatibility, (6) **Latency** — network calls between services, (7) **Infrastructure cost** — more servers, tools, monitoring.

### Q15: Design the microservice architecture for Uber.

**Answer:** Services: (1) **User Service** — rider/driver profiles, (2) **Ride Service** — ride matching, (3) **Location Service** — real-time GPS tracking (write-heavy, use Cassandra), (4) **Pricing Service** — dynamic pricing (surge), (5) **Payment Service** — billing, transactions, (6) **Notification Service** — push/SMS, (7) **ETA Service** — ML-based arrival time. Communication: Location/ride matching via Kafka (high throughput), payment via sync gRPC. Use CQRS for ride history (write to Cassandra, read from Elasticsearch).

**Next Chapter: [Event-Driven Architecture →](02_Event_Driven.md)**
